claims.text: The initial material consists of noble-metal salt precursors adsorbed on a substrate.
Rapid synthesis conditions can produce phase separation and non-uniform nanoparticle morphology.
Slowing the temperature ramp inhibits precursor mobility.
Inhibition of precursor mobility favors formation of single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
Limited precursor mobility reduces atomic diffusion distances and times.
Reduced diffusion minimizes atomic clustering and elemental segregation.
Slowing the temperature increase reduces the kinetic energy available to precursor atoms.
Fast heating promotes rapid nucleation and growth of secondary phases.
Formation of single-phase HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles.
Restricted diffusion favors stochastic but uniform incorporation of the constituent atoms.
A slower ramp will improve elemental homogeneity relative to rapid heating.
A slower ramp will reduce phase separation and elemental segregation relative to rapid heating.
A slower ramp will maintain the targeted single-phase crystal structure.
Changing the ramp rate may modestly alter particle size or morphology.
The rapid-heating baseline operates on millisecond-to-second timescales and can include cooling rates up to approximately 100000 K/s.
Rapid heating and cooling promote high precursor mobility and thereby increase segregation, phase separation, and non-uniform nanoparticle formation.
The proposed ramp-rate intervention applies to noble-metal HEA nanoparticles containing more than five elements.
The intervention is applicable when diffusion kinetics during the thermal ramp can compete with thermodynamic segregation.
The optimal degree of ramp slowing depends on the particular precursors and their decomposition kinetics.

contradictions.description: The intervention lengthens the thermal ramp, while the mediator invokes reduced diffusion time. No explanation is given for how a longer ramp reduces the time available for mobility or diffusion.
The conditions require more than five elements, whereas the boundary expands applicability to five or more elements, inconsistently including five-element alloys.

The mediator and mechanism assert that restricting diffusion produces uniform incorporation, while the uncertainty field acknowledges that sufficient precursor mixing must still occur. The hypothesis does not resolve how reduced interdiffusion simultaneously permits homogeneous alloying.
